title: Daily Temperatures
description: For each day, find how many days until a warmer temperature using a monotonic decreasing stack.

data.text: Given an array of daily temperatures, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the number of days you must wait after day `i` for a warmer temperature. If no warmer day exists, `answer[i]` is `0`.
For each day, look ahead until a warmer temperature appears. O(n²) and repeats comparisons across overlapping ranges.

data.title: Brute force O(n²)

data.text: Keep a stack of indices whose temperature has not yet found a warmer day. The stack is always in decreasing temperature order from bottom to top. For each new day, pop every index whose temperature is lower — the current day is their answer. Push the current day. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the scan is O(n).

data.title: Monotonic stack O(n)
data.content: The stack holds unresolved days in decreasing temperature order.

data.title: How to recognise a monotonic stack problem
data.text: The wording usually contains 'next greater', 'next smaller', 'how many days until', or 'span'. If you need, for each element, the nearest element with a comparison property to one side, a monotonic stack is almost always the intended O(n) solution.

data.title: Strict vs non-strict comparison chooses the variant
data.text: Using `<` here answers 'next strictly warmer'. Switching to `<=` answers 'next warmer or equal'. Many interview follow-ups hinge on exactly this distinction, so state which one you are implementing.

data.caption: Indices wait on the stack in decreasing temperature order until a warmer day pops them and records the gap.

cards.title: Monotonic stack
cons: Invariant takes a moment to see

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The same template solves 'next greater element', 'stock span', 'largest rectangle in a histogram', and 'trapping rain water' (with a stack instead of two pointers). Learning one monotonic stack implementation effectively unlocks all of them.
